---
title: "Rewarding Calibration: RLCD and Proper Scoring Rules"
---

Every reward in the book so far scores the *answer*. A preference model scores how much raters like
it; a verifier scores whether it is right. Neither asks the model how sure it is, and neither rewards
it for knowing. In September 2026 TypeSafe AI announced a training method named for that missing
target, Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), for a model, Jev, that returns typed
decisions with probabilities. Only the name and the goal of RLCD are public. This chapter is
therefore built in three visibly separate layers: what was disclosed, stated and dated; a
first-principles reconstruction of what *rewarding calibration* means as RL, which is this book's own
analysis and not TypeSafe's algorithm; and the openly published research on the same objective. The
reconstruction is where the RL content is. It shows why a correctness reward pushes a model toward
confident guessing, why a proper scoring rule makes honest probabilities optimal, and why the answer
and the confidence cannot be rewarded separately.

## Layer 1: what was disclosed

As of 1 October 2026, the primary source is TypeSafe AI's announcement, "Introducing System One Models
& Jev", dated 15 September 2026 [@typesafe2026jev]. It describes "a new stack entirely focused on
automation: with a new model architecture, parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and training
method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD)". It contrasts RLCD's objective
with RLHF's ("human preference") and RLVR's ("outputs that can be programmatically verified"): RLCD
optimizes for "calibrated decisions: answers with epistemically honest probabilities on System One
tasks". Jev returns "type-safe structured values", with "all answers ... accompanied with calibrated
probabilities and confidence scores", and "outputs all probabilities in parallel instead of
autoregressively generating by token" [@typesafe2026jev].

The announcement does **not** disclose the training algorithm, the reward function or the
architecture. Its FAQ says that Jev "is neither small nor an LLM", that on training data "We make all
the data ourselves" ("if you want to find out more, we'd have to hire you"), and that TypeSafe
"deliberately chose not to publish performance against public benchmarks" [@typesafe2026jev]. Its
performance claims are the vendor's: end-to-end responses in "70ms-500ms", "40x-200x faster for the
same levels of frontier intelligence for System One shaped queries", input tokens at "$0.042 / MTok"
with output tokens "FREE", a model that "can't hallucinate" and "never makes type errors", and
workflow comparisons of "193.6x faster, 444.6x cheaper". The post itself adds caveats: "Extraordinary
claims require extraordinary evidence", the LLM comparison numbers come from OpenRouter where routing
"almost certainly" biases them, and "we can't prove it isn't subsidized" [@typesafe2026jev]. None of
these claims has been independently verified beyond the evaluation below.

**One independent evaluation exists.** Guo et al. benchmark Jev as a zero-shot detector of ten
alignment failures across 44 benchmarks and report a median AUROC of 0.886 with a single generic
question, beating supervised baselines on most benchmarks at 63× lower cost than LLM-judge scorers
[@guo2026justaskjev]. It does not describe RLCD's mechanism. Its calibration findings are the part
that bears on this chapter, and they are more nuanced than "calibrated": "Jev's probabilities are
calibrated when pooled but not within a benchmark." Pooled, the reliability curve is "close to the
diagonal (ECE 0.047)"; per benchmark, "median per-benchmark ECE ... is 0.168 against 0.074 under
perfect calibration, and 24 of 31 benchmarks exceed the null's 95th percentile". The error is "a
base-rate mismatch, not a ranking problem": Jev's mean probability misses a benchmark's positive rate
by a median of 0.125 while ranking well (median AUROC 0.905) [@guo2026justaskjev]. Calibration is a
property of a model *on a distribution*, and one evaluation can show it holding in aggregate and
failing within each slice.

::: {.callout-tip title="Method card — RLCD (TypeSafe AI), public fields only"}
| | |
|---|---|
| **Signal** | "calibrated decisions: answers with epistemically honest probabilities" (the objective is public; the reward is **undisclosed**) |
| **Samples from** ($q$) | undisclosed |
| **Per-sample weight** ($w$) | undisclosed |
| **Stability** | undisclosed |
| **Credit granularity** | undisclosed (outputs are typed decisions with probabilities, produced "in parallel", not token by token) |
| **Models in memory** | undisclosed |
| **Targets** | calibrated probabilities over typed answers (stated goal) |
| **Classical lineage** | undisclosed; see the reconstruction below for what the stated goal implies |
:::

## Layer 2: a first-principles reconstruction

::: {.callout-warning title="A first-principles reconstruction, not the vendor's algorithm"}
Everything in this section is this book's analysis of what it means to reward calibration with RL.
It is built from public theory (proper scoring rules) and checked on the toy language. It is not a
description of how TypeSafe trains Jev, which has not been published.
:::

### The problem with a correctness reward

Start from RLVR: reward $r = \mathbb{1}[\text{correct}]$. If the policy can answer or abstain, abstaining
earns 0 and answering earns $P(\text{correct})$ in expectation, so answering is better whenever that
probability is above zero. A binary correctness reward never rewards "I'm not sure". Wu et al. put
it exactly: standard RLVR "inadvertently incentivize[s] models as good test-takers rather than honest
communicators, encouraging guessing whenever correctness probability exceeds zero"
[@wu2025behaviorally]. And if the policy states a confidence alongside its answer, a correctness
reward is indifferent to it: nothing in the gradient touches the confidence, so it stays wherever
pretraining put it.

### Rewarding the stated probability with a proper scoring rule

Let the policy output an answer $a$ and a confidence $p$ that $a$ is correct, and let
$o = \mathbb{1}[a \text{ correct}]$. Reward the confidence with a scoring rule $S(p, o)$. If $S$ is
**proper**, then for a fixed answer whose true probability of being right is $q$, the expected score
$\mathbb{E}_{o\sim\text{Bernoulli}(q)}[S(p,o)]$ is maximized by reporting $p = q$: honesty is optimal.
The negative Brier score $-(p-o)^2$ and the log score are both strictly proper. The theory of proper
scoring rules is in
[loss-functions-lab's decision-theory chapter](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/loss-functions-lab/chapters/08-decision-theory-proper-scoring.html)
and in Gneiting and Raftery [@gneiting2007strictly]; for the Brier score the check is one line,
$\mathbb{E}[-(p-o)^2] = -\big(q(1-p)^2 + (1-q)p^2\big)$, whose derivative in $p$ vanishes at $p = q$.

Three points make this an RL problem rather than ordinary calibration.

**The label depends on the policy.** The thing the confidence must predict is whether the model's
*own* answer is right. Change the policy's answers and the right confidence changes. The feedback
is evaluative and the data self-generated, the two properties of the
[first chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd). Post-hoc calibration on a fixed dataset of someone
else's answers cannot express this.

**The answer and the confidence interact.** Reward the confidence alone with the Brier score and the
expected reward of an answer with success probability $q$, reported honestly, is $-q(1-q)$. That is
highest at $q = 0$ or $q = 1$: the score rewards answers whose outcome is *predictable*, including
answers that are predictably wrong. Add the correctness term, $r = o - (p - o)^2$, and the expected
reward of an honestly reported answer is $q - q(1-q) = q^2$, increasing in $q$: the policy should
give its best answer and its honest probability of being right.

::: {.callout-note title="Definition — Correctness plus a proper scoring rule"}
$$
r(a, p) = \mathbb{1}[a \text{ correct}] + S(p, \mathbb{1}[a\text{ correct}]),\qquad S(p,o) = -(p - o)^2,
$$
whose expected value for an answer with success probability $q$ is maximized by the best available
answer and $p = q$ (expected value $q^2$ at the optimum).
:::

Damani et al. state the general condition: with a correctness term of weight $\lambda$, a proper
scoring rule keeps both incentives as long as it is *bounded*, $S(p,1) - S(p,0) < \lambda$; an
unbounded rule like the log score can make "incorrect answers with zero confidence" optimal
[@damani2025beyond].

**One decision, an immediate outcome: a contextual bandit.** For a single typed decision whose
outcome is known right away, there is no sequence of states to assign credit across. This is the
contextual bandit of the [first chapter](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd), not a long-horizon MDP, and
the policy gradient of the [policy-gradient chapter](02-policy-gradients.qmd) with a group baseline is
all the machinery needed.

::: {.callout-important title="Classical lineage — this is a contextual bandit with a forecaster's scoring rule"}
The decision problem is Sutton and Barto's associative search: one action per context, an immediate
outcome. The reward is a proper scoring rule, the device weather forecasting has used since Brier to
make honest probability reports optimal. RL contributes the part forecasting did not need: the event
being forecast is the outcome of the learner's own action.
:::

Abstention then falls out. With calibrated probabilities, a decision rule can answer only when the
stated probability clears a threshold set by the cost of a wrong answer. With uncalibrated ones, the
same rule is meaningless.

::: {.callout-tip title="Method card — Correctness + Brier reward (the book's reconstruction)"}
| | |
|---|---|
| **Signal** | the outcome of the policy's own answer, scored by $\mathbb{1}[\text{correct}] - (p - \mathbb{1}[\text{correct}])^2$ |
| **Samples from** ($q$) | $\pi_\theta$: several (answer, confidence) samples per prompt (on-policy) |
| **Per-sample weight** ($w$) | the reward minus a leave-one-out baseline |
| **Stability** | none beyond a small learning rate in the toy; a KL to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is optional |
| **Credit granularity** | one decision, one immediate outcome (contextual bandit) |
| **Models in memory** | policy (+ a verifier for the outcome) |
| **Targets** | the best answer per prompt, with stated probability equal to its success rate |
| **Classical lineage** | a contextual bandit trained by REINFORCE with a Monte Carlo baseline; the reward is a proper scoring rule from forecasting |
:::

### Checked on the toy language

The toy version (`rl4llm/calibration.py`) makes a response an answer (three tokens) followed by a
stated confidence (the last token, one of 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9). Each answer succeeds at random
with a hidden probability, so there is real uncertainty the model cannot resolve. The prompts range
from hard (the best answer is right 23% of the time) to easy (96%), and the reference policy is
overconfident, putting most of its mass on "0.9". The policy is trained by RLOO with three rewards,
and everything in @fig-calibration-reward is computed exactly under the trained policies.

![The answer-plus-confidence task (2,500 steps of RLOO, 16 samples per prompt, median of 3 seeds; exact evaluation). Left: reliability diagrams; marker area shows how often each confidence is stated. Middle: accuracy, expected calibration error, and the rate of answers stated with confidence ≥ 0.7 that are wrong. The binary correctness reward raises accuracy but leaves the overconfident prior in place; the Brier score alone becomes calibrated by drifting toward predictably wrong answers; correctness plus Brier gives nearly the binary reward's accuracy with honest probabilities. Right: accuracy among answered questions when the policy abstains below a confidence threshold. Only the calibrated policy turns abstention into higher accuracy.](../images/calibration_reward.png){#fig-calibration-reward}

The three rewards do what the analysis predicts. The **binary** reward raises accuracy from 0.37 to
0.63 (the best achievable is 0.65) and leaves the stated confidence uninformative: its reliability
curve is flat, its calibration error is 0.33, and 32% of all its answers are stated with confidence of
at least 0.7 and wrong. The **Brier score alone** is the best calibrated (ECE 0.03), but its accuracy
falls to 0.47, because on the hard prompts it learns to give answers that are almost surely wrong and
say "0.1" (the exact optimum of the Brier-only reward is a surely-wrong answer on three of the four
prompts). **Correctness plus Brier** keeps accuracy at 0.61, is calibrated (ECE 0.05), and cuts the
confident-wrong rate from 32% to 7%. The right panel shows why calibration is worth having. Abstaining
below a confidence threshold raises the calibrated policy's accuracy from 0.61 to 0.86 on the half of
the questions it answers; the binary-reward policy's confidence carries so little information that
the same rule only lifts its accuracy from 0.63 to 0.68 at a similar coverage.

## Layer 3: public research on rewarding calibration

Several openly published methods reward calibration with RL. None of them is TypeSafe's method, and
the list reflects what was found by search as of 1 October 2026.

- **RLCR** (Damani et al., 2025) has the model produce reasoning, an answer, an analysis of its
  uncertainty and a numerical confidence, and rewards it with
  $\mathbb{1}_{y\equiv y^*} - (q - \mathbb{1}_{y\equiv y^*})^2$, correctness plus the Brier score, the
  reward reconstructed above. The paper proves that this reward (or any bounded proper scoring rule
  added to correctness) yields answers that are both accurate and calibrated, and reports large
  calibration gains (ECE 0.37 → 0.03 on HotpotQA) with accuracy comparable to standard RL, including
  on held-out datasets where standard RL made calibration worse [@damani2025beyond].
- **Behaviorally calibrated RL** (Wu et al., 2025) argues that hallucination is partly "a predictable
  statistical consequence" of objectives that reward guessing, and trains with strictly proper scoring
  rules so that a model can abstain or flag individual claims; it reports a 4B model surpassing
  frontier models on its uncertainty metrics [@wu2025behaviorally].
- **RefGRPO** (Zhu, 2026) targets agents: it finds a "reflection gap" in which agents mis-assess their
  own outputs after seeing environment feedback, and adds "a free calibration bonus computed by
  contrasting the agent's own reflection with the actual outcome" to standard RL [@zhu2026reflection].
- **OpenJev-RLCD** (Gao and Wang, posted 30 September 2026, not peer-reviewed) is an independent,
  open attempt at "a working implementation of reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions",
  which states that it claims "nothing about Jev's internal algorithm" [@gao2026openjev]. It scores the
  distribution a reasoning model assigns to the options after its rationale with the Brier score. Its
  Proposition 1 is a variance decomposition: scoring the *mixture* over sampled rationales equals the
  average per-rationale score plus a bonus for rationales that disagree, so a policy can collect
  reward by randomizing its conclusions. Its Corollary 1 reads the familiar objective in those terms:
  with sampled one-hot answers the calibrated group reward is "RLVR + Gini bonus", that is,
  $2\Pr(A{=}Y) - 1$ plus the Gini impurity $1 - \|p\|^2$. Both identities are short algebra on the
  Brier score, and the test suite checks them numerically (`tests/test_calibration.py`). The paper's
  conclusion is to score each rationale's own distribution, which removes the bonus. Its empirical
  results are the authors' own, two days old at the time of writing.

### A name collision

"RLCD" also names an unrelated, earlier method: *Reinforcement Learning from Contrastive
Distillation* (Yang et al., 2023), which builds preference pairs by sampling from a positive and a
negative prompt (for example, "harmless" vs. "harmful" instructions) and trains a preference model on
them [@yang2023rlcd]. The two share an acronym and nothing else. The [acronym appendix](../appendix-acronyms.qmd)
lists both.

## Connections

- [What Makes a Problem RL](01-what-makes-a-problem-rl.qmd) explains why rewarding calibration is RL
  and not post-hoc calibration: the confidence must predict the correctness of the model's own,
  changing answers, from evaluative feedback on self-generated data.
- [Where Rewards Come From, and How They Break](05-rewards.qmd) covers rewards learned from what raters
  prefer; this chapter designs a reward whose optimum is provably honest, and shows that even a proper
  scoring rule can be gamed if it is not tied to correctness.
- [Policy Gradients Without a Critic](08-policy-gradients-without-a-critic.qmd) supplies the estimator
  (a group baseline) and, through OpenJev-RLCD's corollary, a new reading of what a group-based RLVR
  objective rewards.
- [Decision Guide and the Unified Table](12-decision-guide.qmd) places calibration rewards on the map
  as a distinct signal source, next to preferences, verifiers and teachers.
